hints: Count all carbons, hydrogens, nitrogens and oxygens in noradrenaline, remembering the benzene ring contributes $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{3}$ when it has three substituents.
walkthrough:
Break the molecule into pieces to count**
Look at noradrenaline as two parts. The disubstituted benzene ring with two $\text{OH}$ groups is $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{3}(\text{OH})_{2}$. The side chain is $-\text{CH}(\text{OH})\text{CH}_{2}\text{NH}_{2}$. Add them together carefully, counting H on each O and N.

Add up to the molecular formula**
Carbons: $6 + 2 = 8$. Hydrogens: $3$ on ring $+ 2$ on phenolic $\text{OH}$ $+ 1+1$ on $\text{CH}(\text{OH})$ $+ 2$ on $\text{CH}_{2}$ $+ 2$ on $\text{NH}_{2} = 11$. So you get $\text{C}_{8}\text{H}_{11}\text{NO}_{3}$.

hints: Focus on the benzylic carbon bearing the $\text{OH}$ group and list the four different groups attached to it.
walkthrough:
Spot the chiral centre**
Find the carbon with the side chain $\text{OH}$. It is bonded to: $\text{OH}$, $\text{H}$, the 3,4-dihydroxyphenyl ring, and $\text{CH}_{2}\text{NH}_{2}$. Four different groups means it is a chiral or asymmetric carbon.

Link chirality to optical isomerism**
A molecule with one chiral centre exists as a pair of non-superimposable mirror images. Those enantiomers rotate plane polarised light in opposite directions, so noradrenaline can show optical isomerism.
Final answer: Yes, noradrenaline shows optical isomerism as it contains a chiral carbon atom bonded to four different groups.

hints: Compare a phenyldiazonium ion, $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{N}_{2}^{+}$, where $-\text{N}_{2}^{+}$ is directly attached to the benzene ring, with an aliphatic diazonium ion.
walkthrough:
See where the positive charge sits**
In the benzenediazonium ion, $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}-\text{N}\equiv\text{N}^{+}$, the $-\text{N}_{2}^{+}$ group is conjugated directly with the pi system of the benzene ring. In an aliphatic diazonium ion from noradrenaline there is no such conjugation.

Explain the stabilising effect**
The pi electrons of the ring can overlap with the diazonium group, so the positive charge is not localised on nitrogen alone but is delocalised and spread over the ring. Delocalisation lowers the energy, giving the aromatic diazonium ion enough stability to exist at $0$ to $5^{\circ}\text{C}$, whereas aliphatic diazonium ions decompose immediately.
Final answer: The phenyldiazonium ion is stabilised because the positive charge is delocalised into the benzene ring and spread over the ring.

hints: Recall the general reaction of a primary aliphatic amine with $\text{HNO}_{2}$: $\text{R-NH}_{2} + \text{HNO}_{2} \rightarrow \text{R-OH} + \text{N}_{2} + \text{H}_{2}\text{O}$.
Apply this to noradrenaline by replacing only the $-\text{CH}_{2}\text{NH}_{2}$ end with $-\text{CH}_{2}\text{OH}$, leaving the benzene ring and its two $\text{OH}$ groups unchanged.
walkthrough:
Recognise the amine type**
The $\text{NH}_{2}$ in noradrenaline is attached to a $\text{CH}_{2}$ group, so it is a primary aliphatic amine. That is completely different chemistry from phenylamine, which is a primary aromatic amine that forms a diazonium salt.

Apply the deamination pattern**
With $\text{HNO}_{2}$, primary aliphatic amines form a very unstable aliphatic diazonium ion that loses $\text{N}_{2}$ at once: $$\text{R-NH}_{2} + \text{HNO}_{2} \rightarrow \text{R-OH} + \text{N}_{2} + \text{H}_{2}\text{O}$$ So the $-\text{NH}_{2}$ is effectively replaced by $-\text{OH}$.

Draw the C, H, O only product**
Keep the 3,4-dihydroxyphenyl part exactly as it is. Change $-\text{CH}(\text{OH})\text{CH}_{2}\text{NH}_{2}$ into $-\text{CH}(\text{OH})\text{CH}_{2}\text{OH}$. That gives $1$-(3,4-dihydroxyphenyl)ethane-1,2-diol, which contains only C, H and O. The other small molecule besides $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$ must be $\text{N}_{2}$ gas.

Final answer: Organic product: $3,4-(\text{HO})_{2}\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{3}\text{CH}(\text{OH})\text{CH}_{2}\text{OH}$, i.e. benzene ring with $\text{OH}$ groups at 3- and 4-positions and side chain $-\text{CH}(\text{OH})\text{CH}_{2}\text{OH}$.
Missing product: $\text{N}_{2}$
Equation: $\text{RCH}_{2}\text{NH}_{2} + \text{HNO}_{2} \rightarrow \text{RCH}_{2}\text{OH} + \text{N}_{2} + \text{H}_{2}\text{O}$ where $\text{R} = 3,4-(\text{HO})_{2}\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{3}\text{CH}(\text{OH})$
